readings.title: Between Asia and Australia: a region apart — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a writer’s comparisons of size and decide what each one is meant to make an English reader see.
readings.focus: How a traveller’s experience corrects a map-reader’s first impression, and the surprising claim the book sets out to prove.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. This is the opening of his first chapter. The Rafflesia has the largest single flower known; Ornithoptera are huge birdwing butterflies; the Isle of Wight is a small island off southern England; Tenasserim is now part of Myanmar, and Celebes is now Sulawesi. Wallace wrote for British readers, so “our possessions” means British colonies.
readings.contentNote: Wallace calls the Malay people “a peculiar and interesting race of mankind,” using the nineteenth-century idea of fixed human races, and calls the orangutan “man-like.”

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter I, “Physical Geography,” from the opening through “Extent of the Archipelago and Islands”; opens “IF we look at a globe or a map of the Eastern hemisphere, we shall perceive between Asia…”; closes “…over which the islands are spread, than to the quantity of land which they contain.”.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Wallace, do so few English readers know this part of the world?
facilitatorNotes: Britain holds few colonies there, few British travellers go, and many maps split the islands between Asia and the Pacific, so the region hardly appears as a whole. Ask what a map’s way of dividing the world can hide.
evidence: Our possessions in it are few and scanty
in many collections of maps it is almost ignored

questions.prompt: Which of Wallace’s comparisons of size works best for you, and why did he choose comparisons like these?
facilitatorNotes: He measures the islands against places his British readers already knew: Borneo could hold the British Isles, Java is about the size of Ireland. Readers today might prefer other measures; the point is to turn numbers into a picture.
evidence: in one of them, Borneo, the whole of the British Isles might be set down
Java, Luzon, and Celebes are each about the size of Ireland

questions.prompt: How does the traveller’s view of the islands differ from the map-reader’s?
facilitatorNotes: On a map they look like scattered pieces of other regions; the traveller sails for weeks along a single coast and comes to see the region as a world of its own. Experience changes the category the islands belong to.
evidence: He sails for days, or even for weeks, along the shores of one of these great islands
He soon comes to look upon this region as one apart from the rest of the world

questions.prompt: What “unexpected fact” does Wallace promise to prove, and why might he state it before telling his travels?
facilitatorNotes: That islands which seem one connected whole divide into two nearly equal parts belonging to two different primary divisions of the earth. Stating it first lets readers watch for the evidence in later chapters; some may feel it would be more exciting to discover it along the way.
evidence: they are divisible into two portions nearly equal in extent
our first impression will be that they form a connected whole

readings.title: Singapore: a crowded port and a square mile of beetles — excerpt
readings.challenge: Sort a crowded description into what Wallace saw, what he was told, and what he concluded.
readings.focus: A port built from many peoples, a missionary’s way of earning trust, and a naturalist’s explanation for an unusually rich patch of forest.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Singapore, an island at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, was then a British trading port. Klings was a period name for South Indian, mostly Tamil, people (Wallace places them in “Western India”); Mahometans are Muslims; Parsees are Zoroastrians whose families came from Persia; praus, junks and sampans are kinds of boats; a joss-house is a Chinese temple. The Chinese man’s “tail” is the long braid the Qing emperors required men to wear. Gambir is a plant used in tanning and dyeing; 30l. means thirty pounds a year; Longicorns are long-horned beetles.
readings.contentNote: Wallace sorts people by origin and judges whole groups, and uses period labels such as “coolie” and “Chinaman” that are now considered offensive. He reports that tigers killed people daily and describes concealed tiger pits.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter II, “Singapore,” the whole chapter; opens “(A SKETCH OF THE TOWN AND ISLAND AS SEEN DURING SEVERAL VISITS FROM 1854 TO 1862.)”; closes “…my first attempts to gain a knowledge of the Natural History of the Malay Archipelago.”.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, how is work divided among Singapore’s peoples? What does this suggest about who held power?
facilitatorNotes: Government, garrison and chief merchants are English; most people, including some of the richest merchants, the farmers and the labourers, are Chinese; Malays are fishermen, boatmen and police; others are clerks, shopkeepers, grooms or sailors. Power sits with the British, though wealth is spread more widely. Readers may question whether any town divides as neatly as his list.
evidence: The government, the garrison, and the chief merchants are English
but the great mass of the population is Chinese

questions.prompt: Find one statement about a particular shop or price and one about a whole people. Which kind could a traveller check?
facilitatorNotes: The price of gimlets is something he could observe and pay; the claim that Klings always overcharge, like the portrait of the merchant who “gets fatter and richer every year,” is a generalization about a group. Discuss how a traveller’s quick judgments can be written to sound like facts.
evidence: You may buy gimlets at a penny each
who almost always ask twice what they are willing to take

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace think the Jesuit missionaries win converts? Which detail about his friend at Bukit-tima best supports the explanation?
facilitatorNotes: Their poverty shows they are sincere. His friend gives away half his rice or half his purse, and when he is in want he asks his flock in return, so trust runs both ways. Some readers may think the school and the help in sickness matter as much as the poverty.
evidence: One secret of the success of these missions is the rigid economy practised in the expenditure of the funds
he would give him half of what he had in the house

questions.prompt: Wallace gives two causes for the many beetles in one square mile of jungle. Which does he stress, and how sure can he be?
facilitatorNotes: Soil, climate and a bright season helped, but he stresses the Chinese woodcutters, whose dead wood, bark and sawdust fed insects and their larvae. “I feel sure” marks a reasoned judgment rather than a tested result: he never compared a patch without woodcutters, though he never found so rich a spot again.
evidence: due in part no doubt to some favourable conditions in the soil, climate, and vegetation
it was also in a great measure dependent, I feel sure, on the labours of the Chinese wood-cutters

readings.title: Malacca: an old port, a mixed town and a butterfly on the road — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Wallace observes from what he judges, and notice how he uses an old book as evidence.
readings.focus: A once-great trading city has shrunk, its peoples keep their own languages and dress, and a single lucky capture shows how much a collector misses.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Malacca (now Melaka, in Malaysia) was seized by the Portuguese in 1511, later held by the Dutch, and by Wallace’s visit in 1854 belonged to Britain. Linschoten (Wallace spells him “Linschott”) was a Dutch traveller whose account of the East was published in the 1590s; Ormuz and Mozambique were Portuguese forts. A lingua-franca is a shared trading language; philological means having to do with the history of languages; Lusitanian means Portuguese; a cravat is a neckcloth; gambir is a plant used in dyeing and tanning; quinine is a medicine for fever. Wallace’s collectors shot birds to preserve their skins.
readings.contentNote: Wallace uses the period word “Chinamen” and calls the Portuguese-descended people of Malacca “a mixed, degraded, and degenerate race,” a prejudiced judgment of his time. Birds are shot for specimens, and Wallace and his servants fall ill with fever.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter III, “Malacca and Mount Ophir,” from the opening to the butterfly at Ayer-panas; opens “(JULY TO SEPTEMBER, 1854.)”; closes “…that a second individual reached this country from the north-western part of Borneo.”.

questions.prompt: How does Wallace use Linschoten’s description, written about 270 years earlier, to show how Malacca has changed?
facilitatorNotes: Linschoten describes ships from all over Asia coming and going “incessantly”; Wallace answers that now hardly a vessel over a hundred tons enters, and the trade is only forest products and fruit. Quoting the old account lets readers measure the fall themselves. Ask what the old account and the new one each leave out.
evidence: This place is the market of all India, of China, of the Moluccas
At present, a vessel over a hundred tons hardly ever enters its port

questions.prompt: Wallace describes the people of Malacca by their languages and their clothes. Which of his statements are observations, and which are judgments? Does he judge only other people?
facilitatorNotes: Observations: who is most numerous, what each group speaks and wears, how the Portuguese verbs have lost their endings. Judgments: the Portuguese descendants are “degraded,” the English hat is “abominable,” Chinese dress cannot be improved. He mocks his own countrymen’s clothes too, but his word for the Portuguese descendants reflects the racial ideas of his time and is not evidence.
evidence: a mixed, degraded, and degenerate race
the abominable hat and cravat

questions.prompt: Wallace calls Malacca Portuguese “ruefully mutilated in grammar” and also “a useful philological phenomenon.” Do these two descriptions agree?
facilitatorNotes: The first is a complaint; the second treats the same change as something interesting to study: one verb form, “Eu vai,” for I go, I went and I will go. Many language scholars today would describe such a language as a new, simpler mixed language rather than a broken one. Students can decide which description the evidence supports.
evidence: ruefully mutilated in grammar
Eu vai, serves for "I go," "I went," or, "I will go."

questions.prompt: How does the story of the butterfly on the forest road support Wallace’s claim that a traveller’s collection is “fragmentary and imperfect”?
facilitatorNotes: He caught the new species only because he happened to see it, guessed it would return to the same spot, and came back next day; he never saw another, and the next specimen reached England twelve years later. One lucky capture shows how many species a collector must miss.
evidence: how fragmentary and imperfect a traveller's collection must necessarily be
I never saw another specimen of it

readings.title: Beetles, a birdwing and a flying frog — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow Wallace’s reasoning about why one place was so rich, and check his numbers and dates as you go.
readings.focus: At a coal-works cut out of the Borneo forest, Wallace collects beetles at an astonishing rate, names a new butterfly, and weighs a workman’s report of a frog that flies.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In 1855 he stayed nine months at new coal-works on the Simunjon River in Sarawak, north-west Borneo. Sarawak was then ruled by Sir James Brooke, an Englishman who had made himself its rajah. The Dyaks are the indigenous peoples of Borneo. Virgin forest has never been cut; a sawpit is a pit over which logs are sawn into planks; Phasmidæ are stick insects; Longicorns are long-horned beetles and Rhynchophora are weevils; antennæ are feelers; a sphinx moth is a hawk-moth, and a trogon a brightly coloured bird; to conjecture is to guess; a membrane is a thin skin; Darwinians follow Charles Darwin’s ideas about how species change over time; Mammalia are mammals.
readings.contentNote: Wallace pays workers to bring him insects, and calls the Chinese workmen “Chinamen,” a word of his time now considered offensive.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from the start of the chapter to the mammals of Simunjon; opens “I ARRIVED at Sarawak on November 1st, 1854, and left it on January 25th, 1856. In the…”; closes “…Bennetti—a rare, otter-like animal, with very broad muzzle clothed with long bristles.”.

questions.prompt: Why was the coal-works such a good place to collect beetles? What two conditions does Wallace name?
facilitatorNotes: A great stretch of untouched forest nearby, and many trees freshly cut and left to rot, which beetles feed on. A small clearing holds more decaying wood than twenty square miles of forest. Readers may notice the irony that cutting the forest made the collecting rich.
evidence: twenty square miles of country may not contain so many fallen and decayed trees as are to be found in any small clearing
secondly upon the quantity of trees that for some months past have been, and which are still being cut down

questions.prompt: What do Wallace’s numbers show about the beetles of Borneo?
facilitatorNotes: He doubled his 320 kinds in under a fortnight, about 24 new species a day, and found some 2,000 kinds, almost all on about a square mile. Nine-tenths of the long-horned beetles were new to science. The numbers make the forest’s variety concrete.
evidence: an average of about 24 new species every day
on scarcely more than a square mile of ground

questions.prompt: Look at the dates in the first paragraphs. Wallace says he went to the coal-works in “March 1865.” What is wrong, and how do you know?
facilitatorNotes: He says he arrived in Sarawak in November 1854 and left in January 1856, so the year must be 1855: a slip, either his or the printer’s. Careful readers check a text against itself; even good books contain errors of this kind.
evidence: I ARRIVED at Sarawak on November 1st, 1854, and left it on January 25th, 1856.
In March 1865 I determined to go to the coal-works

questions.prompt: Wallace never saw the frog fly. Why does he come to believe the workman who said it did?
facilitatorNotes: The frog’s toes are webbed far more than a tree-frog needs for swimming or climbing, so the webs probably have another use. The body supports the testimony: the account “becomes more credible.” He also links it to Darwin’s idea that body parts can be adapted to new uses.
evidence: He assured me that he had seen it come down, in a slanting direction, from a high tree, as if it flew.
it is difficult to imagine that this immense membrane of the toes can be for the purpose of swimming only

readings.title: The Mias: hunting the orang-utan, and a baby in the bog — excerpt
readings.challenge: Read a scientist’s plain account of hunting and decide what his words show about his attitude.
readings.focus: Wallace came to Borneo to study and collect the orang-utan; one hunt leaves him caring for an orphaned baby.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In 1855 Wallace stayed at new coal-works on the Simunjon River in Sarawak, north-west Borneo, partly to study and collect the orang-utan, which the Dyaks, the island’s indigenous people, call the Mias. Museums then wanted skins and skeletons of every animal, and collectors shot them. The Hylobates are gibbons; an 80-bore gun is a small gun; arrack is a strong spirit, used here to preserve a skin; the Derby Museum is in Liverpool. A quill is a hollow feather shaft, used here like a straw.
readings.contentNote: Wallace shoots several orang-utans, including a mother; wounded animals howl, throw branches and fight back. He calls two Dyak youths “young savages,” a contemptuous period word.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from Wallace’s purpose at Simunjon to the first days of feeding the baby; opens “One of my chief objects in coming to stay at Simunjon was to see the Orang-utan (or great…”; closes “…up in disgust, and set up a scream very like that of a baby in similar circumstances.”.

questions.prompt: What were Wallace’s “chief objects” at Simunjon? What did obtaining “good specimens” mean in practice?
facilitatorNotes: To see the orang-utan in the wild, study its habits, and collect specimens of both sexes and all ages. In practice that meant shooting them and preserving their skins and skeletons for museums. Wallace saw this as science; readers today may feel very differently, and the passage lets them think about both.
evidence: to study his habits, and obtain good specimens
which was afterwards purchased for the Derby Museum

questions.prompt: What do the wounded or frightened orang-utans do? What do these details show about the animals, and about Wallace as an observer?
facilitatorNotes: They hide in the leaves, climb again after falling, howl “like a cough,” break off branches and throw them down, and one, with a broken arm, pulls two men towards its mouth. Wallace records behaviour precisely even in the middle of a hunt; the details also show strength and something like rage.
evidence: howling in a strange voice like a cough, and seemed in a great rage
it was too strong for these young savages

questions.prompt: Wallace writes that “to avoid trouble, I shot it through the heart.” What does the phrase “to avoid trouble” reveal?
facilitatorNotes: He reports the killing as a practical step, with no comment on the animal’s suffering. Some readers will find the flatness shocking; others will see it as the ordinary tone of a nineteenth-century collector. Ask whether the plain style makes the scene easier or harder to read.
evidence: and, to avoid trouble, I shot it through the heart

questions.prompt: Find the details that make the baby seem like a human baby. Why might Wallace keep making the comparison?
facilitatorNotes: It clings to his beard, sucks his finger “with great vigour,” and screams “very like that of a baby in similar circumstances.” The ape is called “man-like,” and Wallace is interested in how close it is to people; the comparison also shows his growing tenderness for “my little infant.”
evidence: set up a scream very like that of a baby in similar circumstances
I in vain inquired for any female animal that could suckle my little infant

readings.title: The Mias: raising an orphan orang-utan — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a careful record of a young animal’s behaviour and notice where Wallace moves from describing to interpreting.
readings.focus: A naturalist becomes a nurse, and his record of the baby’s short life mixes affection, comedy and science.
readings.context: Recap: in Borneo Wallace shot orang-utans, or Mias, for museum collections. When he shot a mother, he found her baby in the bog, unhurt, and took it home; with no milk to be had, he fed it rice-water from a bottle. Tenacity is a strong grip; a hare-lip monkey is a kind of macaque; an intermittent fever comes and goes; castor-oil is a medicine; a countenance is a face, and ludicrous means comic.
readings.contentNote: The orphaned baby ape sickens and dies; Wallace then preserves its skin and skeleton and finds bones broken in its fall when its mother was shot.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from the baby’s cradle and bath to its death; opens “When handled or nursed, it was very quiet and contented, but when laid down by itself…”; closes “…hard swellings on the limbs where the irregular junction of the bones had taken place.”.

questions.prompt: List the ways Wallace looks after the baby. Which plan shows the most ingenuity, and why does it fail?
facilitatorNotes: A cradle with a mat washed daily, baths under the spout, brushing, a little ladder for exercise, spoon-feeding, and an “artificial mother” made of buffalo-skin. The skin works until the baby tries to suck and gets mouthfuls of hair, and nearly chokes on wool. No invention can replace what it has lost.
evidence: I endeavoured to make an artificial mother
One day it got some wool into its throat

questions.prompt: Wallace says the baby “began to remember its lost parent.” Is that something he observed, or something he concluded? How could you tell?
facilitatorNotes: He observed that it tried to suck the skin and screamed; “remember its lost parent” is his explanation of that behaviour. It may well be right, or it may be hunger alone. Discuss how much feeling an observer can fairly read into an animal’s actions.
evidence: till it began to remember its lost parent, and try to suck

questions.prompt: What does Wallace learn by putting the young Mias in a box with a monkey of about the same age?
facilitatorNotes: The monkey runs, jumps, examines everything and feeds itself; the Mias lies helpless on its back like a very young baby. The contrast shows that the orang-utan, like a human, has a long, helpless infancy, and makes the Mias look “more baby-like by the comparison.” The comedy of the monkey sitting on its face is part of the record too.
evidence: There could hardly be a greater contrast, and the baby Mias looked more baby-like by the comparison.

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph Wallace mourns “my little pet,” then gives its weight and measurements and preserves its skin. What do you make of this mix of feeling and science? What did he discover about its fall?
facilitatorNotes: Both are sincere: he grieved and he was still a collector, so the body becomes a specimen. Preparing the skeleton showed that the fall from its mother had broken an arm and a leg, which had already healed. Wallace does not comment on what that discovery means; readers may.
evidence: I much regretted the loss of my little pet
when it fell from the tree it must have broken an arm and a leg

readings.title: The Mias: the giant in the tree — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Wallace saw for himself from what he was told, and look for evidence that supports the report.
readings.focus: Wallace hunts, measures and preserves a huge male orang-utan, and records a Dyak account of a Mias that fought back.
readings.context: Recap: at the Simunjon coal-works in Borneo, Wallace shot orang-utans, which the Dyaks call the Mias, for museum collections. He found a baby beside its dead mother and tried to raise it; it died after about three months. Now he goes back to a week after he found the baby. Entomologising is collecting insects; a ball is a bullet; “Tuan” is Malay for “sir”; creepers and jungle ropes are climbing plants; Mias Chappan or Pappan is a Dyak name for the large orang with a fold of skin on each side of the face; the Derby Museum is in Liverpool; to lacerate is to tear; decomposition is rotting. In the 1850s naturalists collected by shooting; today orang-utans are protected and critically endangered.
readings.contentNote: Wallace shoots a large orang-utan many times and lists its wounds; an orang-utan badly bites a Dyak man and is killed with spears. Wallace calls the Chinese workers “Chinamen,” a word of his time now considered offensive.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from the shooting of the first full-grown male to the skull of the Mias killed by the Dyaks; opens “Exactly a week after I had caught this interesting little animal I succeeded in shooting…”; closes “…the bone, but the skull was a very fine one, and the teeth remarkably large and perfect.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the big Mias so hard to shoot and to bring down? List the difficulties.
facilitatorNotes: He hides where leaves are thick, moves fast and silently, settles in a fork where he cannot fall, and the cut tree is held up by creepers. Even the Dyaks fear to climb to him. Wallace’s plain list of problems shows how much skill and labour the collecting took.
evidence: the Mias had a knack of selecting places with dense foliage beneath
it was so held up by jungle ropes and climbers to adjoining trees that it only fell into a sloping position

questions.prompt: Wallace measures the dead Mias exactly. What do his numbers show, and why would a naturalist need them?
facilitatorNotes: The arms span over seven feet though the animal stands only four feet two inches, so its legs are very short and its arms very long. Exact figures let him compare specimens and test travellers’ tales of giant apes, which he does later in the chapter.
evidence: His outstretched arms measured seven feet three inches across
the legs being exceedingly short in proportion

questions.prompt: “Yet he was still alive when he fell.” Why do you think Wallace includes this, and how does the paragraph make you feel?
facilitatorNotes: He is amazed at the animal’s strength (note his exclamation mark), and he records the wounds as facts. He does not express regret. Readers may feel admiration, pity or anger; ask how a naturalist today might study the same animal.
evidence: Both legs were broken, one hip-joint and the root of the spine completely shattered
Yet he was still alive when he fell.

questions.prompt: The story of the Dyak man who was bitten comes from other people. How far can Wallace trust it, and what does he find that supports it?
facilitatorNotes: It is testimony: “some Dyaks came to tell us.” But he gets the dead Mias the next day and finds “a great gash in his face,” a trace that fits a fight with spears and choppers. Testimony and physical evidence together make the account believable.
evidence: some Dyaks came to tell us
There was a great gash in his face

readings.title: The Mias: a nest at the top of the forest — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice what Wallace finds “interesting” and what he leaves out, and judge his reasons.
readings.focus: A wounded orang-utan builds a nest at the top of a tree; Wallace waits months for its skeleton, and travels by flooded river in search of more.
readings.context: Recap: in Borneo Wallace shot a huge male orang-utan, measured it and preserved its skeleton, and heard from the Dyaks of a Mias that tore a man’s arm before it was killed. An arillus is a fleshy covering on a seed, like the mace around a nutmeg; the cervical vertebrae are the bones of the neck; necrophagous beetles feed on dead bodies; a pupa-case is the shell an insect leaves after changing to its adult form; an ulcer is an open sore; medicated arrack is strong spirit used to preserve skins; Macacus cynomolgus, Semnopithecus and Nasalis larvatus are scientific names for a macaque, a leaf-monkey and the proboscis monkey; screw-pines are palm-like plants.
readings.contentNote: Wallace shoots several more orang-utans, leaves one to rot in a tree for months, and kills a young one he does not bother to collect. He again calls Chinese workers “Chinamen,” a word now considered offensive.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from the male shot on June 18th to the journey up the river to Semábang; opens “On June 18th I had another great success, and obtained a fine adult male. A Chinaman told…”; closes “…filled up the channel, making our journey a constant succession of difficulties.”.

questions.prompt: How does the wounded Mias build its nest? What does Wallace find “very interesting” about it?
facilitatorNotes: With one good arm it breaks off boughs and lays them “across and across” until it is hidden in a compact mass of leaves, in a few minutes. Wallace admires the choice of place and the speed. The observation is valuable even though it happens during a hunt.
evidence: breaking off good-sized boughs with the greatest ease, and laying them back across each other
a compact mass of foliage, which entirely concealed him from our sight

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace refuse to double his offer to the men who could cut down the tree? What does his reason tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: He means to stay for months and fears that paying too much once would raise every future price. It is careful business sense; it also costs him the skin, which rots. Readers may call it sensible, stingy, or both.
evidence: Had I doubled my offer, they would probably have accepted it
it would not have answered to begin paying too exorbitantly

questions.prompt: What happens to the body left in the tree, and what does Wallace get from it in the end?
facilitatorNotes: Flies and beetles clean it for months while sun and rain dry it; finally he gets a perfect skeleton missing one wrist-bone, perhaps taken by a lizard. Even here he notes the insects as a naturalist would: “millions” of pupa-cases and “thousands” of beetles.
evidence: millions of the pupa-cases of flies and other insects
the skeleton was perfect, except one small wrist-bone

questions.prompt: Wallace says young animals are “of comparatively little interest.” Interesting to whom? What do you think of his choice?
facilitatorNotes: To a collector describing species, adult specimens show the full size and features, so a young one is less useful to a museum. But he has killed it and leaves it in the tree. Students may judge this harshly by today’s standards; ask them to say what standard they are using.
evidence: as young animals are of comparatively little interest, I did not have the tree cut down to get it

readings.title: The Mias: a bamboo ladder and a puzzle of size — excerpt
readings.challenge: Test each of Wallace’s conclusions against the evidence he gives for it.
readings.focus: Wallace finds what he believes is a second kind of orang, watches Dyaks climb a smooth tree by a bamboo ladder, and draws a conclusion about how orang-utans grow.
readings.context: Recap: Wallace has been shooting orang-utans in Borneo for museum collections, noting how they build nests and travel through the trees. After weeks laid up with an injured ankle, he set off up a flooded river to Semábang, where there was said to be a large Dyak house and plenty of orangs. A verandah is a covered platform along a house; edible birds’-nests are made into soup; the Durian and the mangosteen (here “Mangusteen”) are tropical fruits; canines and incisors are kinds of teeth; a protuberance is a bulge, and lateral means at the side; the cranium is the skull; Professor Richard Owen was a leading anatomist in London; Simia morio is the name he gave to a supposed smaller orang; Mias-kassir is a Dyak name; a benefactor is someone who does good to others; ingenuity is cleverness.
readings.contentNote: Wallace shoots more orang-utans, including females and young ones. He sees baskets of dried human heads kept as trophies from past wars, and uses words of his time such as “natives.” Dogs are kept half-starved.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from the Dyak house at Semábang to the measuring of the oldest male; opens “Near the landing-place we found a fine house, 250 feet long, raised high above the ground…”; closes “…the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, rarely if ever exceeds 4 feet 2 inches.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace think the Semábang Mias is “a different kind”? Could there be another explanation for what he saw?
facilitatorNotes: It is a full-grown male (its teeth prove it) but has no fold on the face and is about a tenth smaller, with broader incisors like Owen’s Simia morio. Another explanation is that males differ with age: Wallace himself ends the chapter by suggesting the face keeps widening as a male grows old. Scientists today know that some adult males never grow the cheek flaps, or grow them late, so this was the same species.
evidence: a full-grown male by its fully developed teeth and very large canines
it had no sign of the lateral protuberance on the face, and was about one-tenth smaller

questions.prompt: How do the two young Dyaks climb a smooth tree with no branches for fifty feet? Why does Wallace call the ladder “perfectly safe”?
facilitatorNotes: They drive bamboo pegs into the trunk, tie a long bamboo pole to them with bark cord, and climb peg by peg, adding pole to pole. If one peg fails, the pole spreads the strain to the pegs above and below. Wallace, who expected them to fall, is “exceedingly struck by the ingenuity,” and now understands pegs he had seen in other trees.
evidence: the strain would be thrown on several others above and below it
I was exceedingly struck by the ingenuity of this mode of climbing

questions.prompt: Other writers had doubted that orang-utans throw branches. How does Wallace defend the claim, and how does he explain why only females did it?
facilitatorNotes: He saw it himself on at least three occasions. His explanation, that a mother defends her young while the strong male fears nothing, is offered as a possibility: “it may be.” He separates what he observed from what he guesses.
evidence: This habit of throwing down branches when irritated has been doubted
the parental instinct of the female leads her to adopt this mode of defending herself and her young ones

questions.prompt: From the oldest male, what does Wallace conclude about how orang-utans grow? Is his evidence enough?
facilitatorNotes: The old male stands no taller than the others but has longer arms and a much wider face, so Wallace thinks arms and face keep growing with age while height stops at about four feet two inches. He measured only a few animals, and he says only that he is “inclined to believe”: a careful conclusion that more specimens could test.
evidence: the immense broad face was 13½ inches wide
I am inclined to believe, therefore

readings.title: How the Mias lives — excerpt
readings.challenge: Test each of Wallace’s explanations against the evidence he gives for it, including the evidence of other people.
readings.focus: Wallace explains where the orang-utan lives, how it moves, sleeps and eats, and weighs what the Dyak chiefs told him.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In Borneo Wallace studied the orang-utan, which the Dyaks call the Mias, and shot several for museum collections. After describing the last one, he gives this sketch of its way of life. Saráwak, Sambas and Sádong are river districts of north-west Borneo; virgin forest has never been cut; the Nipa is a palm of tidal swamps, and second-growth jungle grows where land was once cleared. An arillus is a fleshy covering on a seed; the Durian is a large spiny fruit; pandanus is a plant with long leaves. Orang Kaya is a chief’s title. The tertiary period was the long age before the Ice Age; Quadrumana (four-handed) was an old name for monkeys and apes. Wallace wrote ten years after Darwin’s Origin of Species, whose idea of natural selection he had reached independently.
readings.contentNote: Wallace mentions fetching his gun to shoot the animals he watched, and Dyak chiefs describe orang-utans killing crocodiles and pythons. He compares the apes’ ease in the treetops to “the Indian on the prairie, or the Arab on the desert,” a period comparison.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from Wallace’s sketch of the animal’s range and habits to his hope for its fossil history; opens “As this was the last Mias I shot, and the last time I saw an adult living animal, I will…”; closes “…past history and earliest appearance of the great man-like apes be at length made known.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the Mias common in Sádong but absent from the Saráwak valley? Explain Wallace’s reasoning.
facilitatorNotes: It lives only in low, swampy land covered with continuous tall forest, through which it can travel from tree-top to tree-top. Saráwak’s swamps are mostly Nipa palm and its drier land is broken by clearings, so it lacks that forest. He explains an “apparent anomaly” by comparing the two places.
evidence: a wide extent of unbroken and equally lofty virgin forest is necessary to the comfortable existence of these animals
the lower portion though swampy is not covered with continuous lofty forest

questions.prompt: How does a Mias cross from one tree to the next? Which details show that Wallace watched closely?
facilitatorNotes: It walks along branches on its knuckles, chooses boughs that mingle with the next tree, grasps them, “seems to try their strength,” and swings across. It never jumps, yet keeps pace with a running man below. Such small steps come only from repeated watching.
evidence: seizing the opposing boughs, grasps them together with both hands, seems to try their strength
He never jumps or springs, or even appears to hurry himself

questions.prompt: Wallace doubts that each Mias makes a fresh nest every night. What is his reasoning, and is it convincing?
facilitatorNotes: If they did, deserted nests would be everywhere; he saw only a few. It is a fair argument from missing evidence, but later observers report that orang-utans usually do build a new nest each night, and old nests may rot quickly in wet forest. A good example of how a reasonable inference can still be wrong.
evidence: Each Mias is said to make a fresh one for himself every night; but I should think that is hardly probable

questions.prompt: Wallace calls pictures of the Mias walking with a stick “entirely imaginary,” but reports the Dyak chiefs’ stories of fights with crocodiles “nearly in the words of my informants.” How does he treat each kind of evidence?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects the pictures because his own observation contradicts them. The chiefs have lived among the animals all their lives, so he records their testimony carefully and calls it “curious,” without claiming to have seen such fights. Students can decide how much weight each deserves.
evidence: Representations of its walking with a stick are entirely imaginary.
I give them nearly in the words of my informants

questions.prompt: What does Wallace hope the caves and rocks of the tropics will one day show? What idea lies behind his hope?
facilitatorNotes: The “forerunners” of the great apes, since other animals had extinct relatives in earlier ages. Behind it is the idea that living species descend from earlier, related forms, the theory of evolution he shared with Darwin.
evidence: we have every reason to believe that the Orang-utan, the Chimpanzee, and the Gorilla have also had their forerunners

readings.title: Is there an orang as big as a gorilla? — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that tests reports against measurements, and notice how carefully its conclusion is worded.
readings.focus: Wallace examines every claim of a giant orang-utan and shows why each one fails.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In Borneo he studied the orang-utan, which the Dyaks call the Mias, and shot and measured many for museum collections. Some travellers reported orangs as big as a gorilla, the African ape, which can stand nearly six feet tall. Temminck, Schlegel, Müller and Blyth were naturalists who measured orangs for museums in Holland and India; Spenser St. John was a British official in Borneo who wrote a travel book; Sir James Brooke was the English rajah of Sarawak; callosities are thick pads of skin; palpably means obviously; a genus is a group of closely related species; “mode of progression” means way of moving; a curator looks after a museum’s collection.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter IV, “Borneo—The Orang-utan,” from “I will now say a few words” to the end of the chapter; opens “I will now say a few words as to the supposed existence of a Bornean Orang as large as…”; closes “…reliable evidence of the existence of Orangs in Borneo more than 4 feet 2 inches high.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence does Wallace give that full-grown male orangs stand about four feet two inches?
facilitatorNotes: He measured seventeen freshly killed orangs himself, kept many skeletons, and found the adult males varied by only an inch. Other naturalists’ measurements, from over a hundred specimens, agree. The evidence is large, careful and checked by others.
evidence: I have myself examined the bodies of seventeen freshly-killed Orangs, all of which were carefully measured
The dimensions given by other naturalists closely agree with mine.

questions.prompt: What do the reports of much larger orangs from Temminck and Mr. St. John have in common?
facilitatorNotes: No one can check them: Temminck’s specimen “never seems to have reached Holland,” and the giant head was not preserved. A claim with no surviving specimen cannot be measured again, and Wallace says “Unfortunately” each time.
evidence: Unfortunately, it never seems to have reached Holland
Unfortunately, even this skull appears not to have been preserved

questions.prompt: How does Wallace show that the measurements in Sir James Brooke’s letter contain a mistake? Which mistake does he think likelier, and why?
facilitatorNotes: In every orang the arm-span is far larger than the height, so a height of 4 feet 6 inches with arms of only 6 feet 1 inch is impossible for an orang. Either the arms are two feet out or the height one foot; height is easier to misjudge. (The letter itself shows how easily numbers slip: dated October 1857, it reports an animal killed in “1867.”)
evidence: there is palpably one error
The latter error is certainly the easiest to make

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace tell the story of the Sumatran orang that sailors thought was seven feet tall? How carefully is his final conclusion worded?
facilitatorNotes: It shows how excitement and fear make a live animal look huge: its skin turns out to be about four feet. His conclusion is not that giant orangs are impossible, only that there is not “the least reliable evidence” for them “up to this time.” A good scientist leaves room for new evidence.
evidence: How easy it is to be deceived in the height of these animals
we have not the least reliable evidence of the existence of Orangs in Borneo more than 4 feet 2 inches high

readings.title: The Durian, king of fruits — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how a writer describes a taste his readers have never tried, and follow one fruit to a general lesson.
readings.focus: Delight in a strange fruit becomes evidence against the idea that nature is arranged for human convenience.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. He is finishing a journey through the interior of Saráwak, in north-west Borneo, among the Dyaks, the island’s inland peoples. Linschott and Paludanus were travel writers of about 1600. Mangosteen, rambutan and lansat are other tropical fruits; carpels are the sections of a fruit; subacid means slightly sour; the Brazil-nut fruit is a hard, heavy pod packed with Brazil nuts.
readings.contentNote: A falling Durian can wound or kill; Wallace describes the wound and a chief struck on the head. His explanation of why such wounds rarely kill reflects nineteenth-century medical ideas.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter V, “Borneo—Journey in the Interior,” from the return to Saráwak through the paragraphs on the Durian; opens “I slept that night in the village of the Sebungow Dyaks, and the next day reached…”; closes “…do not appear to be organized with exclusive reference to the use and convenience of man.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Wallace dislike the Durian in Malacca but love it in Borneo?
facilitatorNotes: In a house the smell is often “so offensive” that people never taste it; in Borneo he found a ripe fruit on the ground and ate it outdoors. Ripeness and setting changed the experience. Ask whether readers have changed their minds about a food in a similar way.
evidence: This was my own case when I first tried it in Malacca
eating it out of doors, I at once became a confirmed Durian eater

questions.prompt: Wallace calls the flavour “indescribable,” then describes it. How does he do it, and does it work?
facilitatorNotes: He starts from something familiar, a custard flavoured with almonds, adds surprising “incongruities” such as cream-cheese and onion-sauce, and ends by saying what the fruit is not. The strange mixture may make readers doubt it or want to try it; both responses fit the text.
evidence: A rich butter-like custard highly flavoured with almonds gives the best general idea of it
It is neither acid, nor sweet, nor juicy

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace stop short of calling the Durian the best of all fruits?
facilitatorNotes: He sorts fruits into two kinds: rich, exquisite foods and refreshing, juicy ones. The Durian cannot replace an orange’s cooling quality, so he crowns the two together. The qualification shows him judging by kinds rather than on a single scale.
evidence: It would not, perhaps, be correct to say that the Durian is the best of all fruits
I should certainly choose the Durian and the Orange as the king and queen of fruits

questions.prompt: What two lessons does Wallace draw from heavy fruits that fall from tall trees? Do you agree with the second?
facilitatorNotes: First, not to generalize from a narrow view of nature, as poets did from English trees; second, that fruits do not seem made for people’s use and convenience. Readers may agree, or argue that a fruit people love and a fruit that can hurt them are both side effects of how the tree lives; the text supports doubting a world arranged for humans.
evidence: not to draw general conclusions from a very partial view of nature
do not appear to be organized with exclusive reference to the use and convenience of man

readings.title: Temples in the Javanese forest — excerpt
readings.challenge: Separate what Wallace saw himself from what he took from another book, and weigh the judgments he adds to his facts.
readings.focus: Ruins raise questions about a vanished society, and Wallace’s answers show both admiration and the prejudices of his time.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In Java, then ruled by the Netherlands, he rides through forest toward Wonosalem, a village on a mountain’s lower slopes. His “Brambanam” is the Hindu temple group now called Prambanan, and “Borobodo” the great Buddhist monument now called Borobudur; both were built in the ninth century, and later Javanese kingdoms went on building temples into the 1400s. Sir Stamford Raffles, a British governor of Java, published a History of Java in 1817. A bas-relief is a carving that stands out from a flat surface; trachytic rock is a hard volcanic stone.
readings.contentNote: Wallace says a “highly artistic and constructive race” was replaced by one “very far its inferior,” and that the present inhabitants look on the ruins “with ignorant amazement”: nineteenth-century racial and cultural judgments, not facts.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter VII, “Java,” from the ruined tomb on the road to Wonosalem through Wallace’s account of the island’s ruins; opens “The road to Wonosalem led through a magnificent forest, in the depths of which we passed…”; closes “…for the collection of the fine sculptures which are everywhere scattered over the land.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the tomb on the road to Wonosalem so striking to come upon?
facilitatorNotes: It appears suddenly on a small rise beside the road, carved and ruined, overgrown with creepers and shadowed by enormous trees. The meeting of careful stonework and wild forest produces the solemn beauty he describes.
evidence: as the traveller comes suddenly upon it on a small elevation by the roadside
overrun with plants and creepers

questions.prompt: Most of this passage describes ruins Wallace never visited. Where does he say so, and why does he break his own rule?
facilitatorNotes: He admits it is against “the plan of this book” and takes his account from Raffles, because he wants wealthy explorers to record the sculptures before they are lost. His numbers are second-hand, which matters when judging them.
evidence: It is altogether contrary to the plan of this book to describe what I have not myself seen
perchance to excite wealthy amateurs to explore them thoroughly

questions.prompt: How does Wallace try to make Borobodo’s size and labour imaginable?
facilitatorNotes: He gives measurements, counts about four hundred figures, adds up nearly three miles of carved wall, and sets the work above the Great Pyramid. Readers can say which method works best; the exclamation mark shows his own astonishment.
evidence: which must therefore occupy an extent of nearly three miles in length!
The amount of human labour and skill expended on the Great Pyramid of Egypt sinks into insignificance

questions.prompt: Wallace calls the change in Java a law of progress that “looks so like retrogression.” What in his account is fact, and what is judgment?
facilitatorNotes: Fact: people who are gone built these temples, and villagers now live in bamboo houses and tell of giants and demons. Judgment: that the newcomers are “very far its inferior,” and that religious ideas explain the change. Readers may suggest other causes, such as war, new rulers or new faiths; Wallace himself says the society behind the temples may “ever remain a mystery.”
evidence: which looks so like retrogression
What could have been the state of society, what the amount of population, what the means of subsistence which rendered such gigantic works possible

readings.title: Leaping monkeys, a gliding lemur and a walled-up hornbill — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice when Wallace measures, when he estimates, and when he relies on what others tell him.
readings.focus: Animals of the Sumatran forest, watched by a collector who sometimes regrets what he does to them.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. At Lobo Raman, a village with a guard-house in eastern Sumatra, he watches the animals around him. The Siamang is a large gibbon; the Galeopithecus or “flying lemur,” now called a colugo, is a gliding mammal and not a true lemur; marsupials are pouched mammals such as kangaroos; prehensile means able to grip. A rupee was a silver coin. Hornbills are large forest birds with enormous beaks.
readings.contentNote: Wallace beats a captive Siamang that bit him and says he regretted it; the animal later dies. Animals are shot for specimens, including a mother flying lemur carrying her baby and a male hornbill killed while feeding its mate.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter VIII, “Sumatra,” from the monkeys at Lobo Raman to the end of the chapter; opens “In Sumatra, monkeys are very abundant, and at Lobo Raman they used to frequent the trees…”; closes “…and is one of those strange facts in natural history which are "stranger than fiction."”.

questions.prompt: What happens when the leader of the monkeys makes a big leap? What makes the scene funny?
facilitatorNotes: The leader jumps boldly, the rest follow nervously, and the last ones hesitate until, afraid of being left behind, they fling themselves into the air and sometimes crash to the ground. The comedy comes from very human-looking hesitation.
evidence: as if in desperation at being left alone, they throw themselves frantically into the air
often go crashing through the slender branches and fall to the ground

questions.prompt: Wallace admits beating the Siamang. Why might he include this, and what does the result show?
facilitatorNotes: He lost patience after a sharp bite; afterwards the Siamang disliked him more than ever while it played for hours with his Malay boys. Telling it shows honesty and regret, and the outcome suggests the animal remembered how it was treated. Readers may judge him harshly or notice that he judges himself.
evidence: I lost patience and gave it rather a severe beating, which I regretted afterwards
It would allow my Malay boys to play with it

questions.prompt: What does Wallace measure when he watches the flying lemur glide, and what does he conclude?
facilitatorNotes: He paces seventy yards between the trees and estimates a drop of no more than thirty-five or forty feet. Landing exactly on a trunk after so long a glide suggests the animal can steer. The distance is paced but the drop only estimated, so “I think proves” is a reasoned conclusion rather than a certain one.
evidence: I paced the distance from the one tree to the other, and found it to be seventy yards
This I think proves that the animal must have some power of guiding itself through the air

questions.prompt: Wallace had “often read” about hornbills walling up their mates. How much of the hornbill story did he see, and how much was he told?
facilitatorNotes: A hunter said he shot the male while it was feeding the female; Wallace went to the tree, saw the small hole and the mud, heard the bird and saw its beak, but was only “assured” that the mud had sealed a larger opening, and the bird and chick were fetched after he left. He mixes his own observation with trusted reports, as much natural history does.
evidence: which one of them assured me he had shot while feeding the female
which I was assured had been used in stopping up the large hole

readings.title: The Rajah’s census: rice that goes missing — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a ruler’s reasoning: what he knows, what he cannot prove, and why the obvious method would fail.
readings.focus: A problem of honest counting, set up as carefully as a puzzle before its solution.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Lombock (now Lombok), the island east of Bali, was ruled by a Rajah, or king, from his capital, Mataram. Wallace tells this chapter like a tale, in a style unlike the rest of his book. A census is an official count of people; tribute is a tax paid to a ruler. A Kapala kampong is a village head, a Waidono a district officer, and a Gusti a prince. A kris is a dagger with a wavy blade; betel nut and sirih leaf are chewed together; Gunong means mountain, and the “great fire mountain” is the island’s volcano.
readings.contentNote: Wallace mocks the Rajah’s thinking (“as hard as a Malay Rajah can be expected to think”), a period ethnic sneer. A visiting captain with a squint is nearly killed because the court fears his “evil eye”; cock-fighting is mentioned, and cattle are slaughtered for the journey.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XII, “Lombock: How the Rajah Took the Census,” from the opening to the chiefs’ camp at Mataram; opens “THE Rajah of Lombock was a very wise man, and he showed his wisdom greatly in the way he…”; closes “…fires frighted away the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues.”.

questions.prompt: How does the rice go missing? Trace it from the villages to the Rajah’s storehouses.
facilitatorNotes: Each level takes a little: the village head excuses the poor and keeps his own granary full, the Waidonos in debt help themselves, and the princes do the same. Small, often excusable takings add up to a shrinking tribute. Ask which taking seems most forgivable.
evidence: it had to pass through many hands before it reached the Government storehouses
the quantity was found to be less each year than the one before

questions.prompt: What does the Rajah notice that shows the officials’ excuses are false? Why can he still do nothing?
facilitatorNotes: The villages look full and well fed in spite of claims of sickness and failed crops, and his chiefs’ kris handles change from wood to ivory to gold. He knows where the rice goes but cannot prove who took it: strong circumstantial evidence, not proof.
evidence: the handles that were of yellow wood were changed for ivory, and those of ivory were changed for gold
But as he could not prove it he kept silence

questions.prompt: Why would an ordinary census fail, according to the Rajah’s reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: Officers sent to count would guess the purpose and make the count match last year’s rice. To work, nobody may know that a count is being taken at all. The problem shows how a measurement can be corrupted by the people who make it.
evidence: the census would be sure to agree exactly with the quantity of rice he got last year
no one must know that there was any census taken at all

questions.prompt: The Rajah announces a dream. What clues suggest it may be a plan rather than a vision?
facilitatorNotes: It arrives just after days of brooding over an unsolved problem, and its commands gather every village and every man of rank. Readers do not yet know the plan, so some may take the dream at face value; the chapter’s first sentence, praising the Rajah’s wisdom in taking the census, invites suspicion.
evidence: he showed his wisdom greatly in the way he took the census
now the trouble is cleared away, for I have had a dream

readings.title: The Rajah’s census: needles for the sacred krisses — excerpt
readings.challenge: Work out the Rajah’s plan before he explains it, then judge what it cost the people who obeyed.
readings.focus: A clever solution that works by turning people’s own beliefs into a counting machine.
readings.context: Recap: the Rajah of Lombock knew his officials were keeping back the rice tax but could not prove it, and an open count of his people would be falsified. After days of brooding he announced that the spirit of the great fire mountain had called him to its summit, and the whole island cleared a road and prepared for the journey. Waringin trees are banyans; the “white-skinned Hollanders” are the Dutch.
readings.contentNote: The Rajah deceives his people with a false religious message, and the tale mentions his power to kill officials who cheat a second time. Hunters shoot deer and wild cattle for the procession’s meals.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XII, “Lombock: How the Rajah Took the Census,” from the procession to the end of the chapter; opens “In the morning a great procession was formed to conduct the Rajah to the mountain. And…”; closes “…head men with heavy hearts, but still with all honour,—for was not the fault their own?”.

questions.prompt: What actually happens at the top of the mountain, and how does the storyteller let readers know?
facilitatorNotes: The Rajah leaves the two boys under a rock, they fall asleep, and he goes a little way off and falls asleep too; the repeated warm, pleasant sun makes the comedy plain. His later report of a trance and a golden-faced spirit contradicts what readers saw.
evidence: and he too fell asleep
he had fallen into a trance, and the great spirit had appeared to him with a face like burnished gold

questions.prompt: How do the needles work as a census, and why does nobody suspect it?
facilitatorNotes: Every village must send one needle per person, so the Rajah gets an exact head count, labelled by village. Because the needles are to make sacred krisses against plague, people fear that one missing needle will doom them, and count with great care. Their own belief makes the count accurate.
evidence: a needle for every head in the village
for they feared that if but one were wanting the whole village would suffer

questions.prompt: How does the Rajah use the needles at harvest time? Why does he speak “mildly”?
facilitatorNotes: He compares each village’s tribute with its needles and tells short-paying chiefs to go back and find who has not paid. He accuses no one directly; the chiefs understand him, and fear does the rest the following year.
evidence: The needles which you sent from your village were many more than came from such-a-one's village, yet your tribute is less than his
for they feared that the Rajah might justly kill those who a second time kept back the right tribute

questions.prompt: The chapter ends: “for was not the fault their own?” Whose reasoning is this, and how does Wallace want readers to take it?
facilitatorNotes: It repeats the villagers’ reasoning: when a kris fails, they blame a miscounted needle, never the kris, so the scheme can never be disproved. Wallace tells it with irony. Readers may admire the Rajah’s cleverness, condemn the deception, or point out that the officials cheated first; the opening called this wisdom, and the ending lets readers question the word.
evidence: for was not the fault their own?
everybody was convinced that there had been a mistake in the number of needles sent from that village

readings.title: The bee-hunter of Timor — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a skilled task step by step, and notice where the observer admits he cannot explain what he sees.
readings.focus: Local skill that outruns a scientist’s understanding, and Wallace’s attempt to account for it.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Timor, a dry island east of Java, was divided between Dutch and Portuguese rulers; Delli (now Dili) was the Portuguese capital. Sandal-wood is a fragrant wood burned as incense. Apis dorsata, the giant honey bee of southern Asia, builds single huge combs in the open air. A bush-rope or creeper is a long woody vine; stupified means stunned; pertinaciously means stubbornly.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XIII, “Timor,” from the island’s soil and exports to the end of the chapter; opens “The soil seems very poor, consisting chiefly of decomposing clayey shales; and the bare…”; closes “…pain and learn to bear it impassively, as without doing so no man could be a bee-hunter.”.

questions.prompt: What preparations do the bee-hunters make before the climb?
facilitatorNotes: One man splits a tough stem and wraps it in palm leaves as a torch, wraps cloth around his loins, head, neck and body but leaves his face, arms and legs bare, and carries a thin cord; a companion ties the lit torch and a knife to a long creeper. Each item has a job later in the climb.
evidence: leaving his face, arms, and legs completely bare
to one end of which the wood-torch was fastened, and lighted at the bottom, emitting a steady stream of smoke

questions.prompt: How does the climber use the creeper to walk up a smooth trunk with no branches for seventy feet?
facilitatorNotes: He loops it around the trunk, holds one end in each hand, sets his feet against the bark and leans back, jerking the loop higher whenever he finds a hold. Wallace stresses skill in using every tiny unevenness of the bark.
evidence: he set his foot against the trunk, and leaning back began walking up it
the slightest irregularities of the bark

questions.prompt: Find two places where Wallace says he could not understand what he saw. Why are these admissions valuable?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot see how the man got onto the branch with both hands holding the creeper, or how he bore the stings so calmly. An honest observer marks the limits of what he knows instead of inventing an answer, and the admissions show the bee-hunter’s skill outrunning the scientist’s understanding.
evidence: in a manner quite unintelligible to me
how he bore their stings so coolly, and went on with his work at that giddy height so deliberately, was more than I could understand

questions.prompt: What explanation does Wallace finally offer for the bee-hunters’ safety? Does his own experience support it?
facilitatorNotes: Slow, deliberate movement and no attempt to escape may make a bee treat a still person like a tree; Wallace himself ran and was chased for half a mile. He adds that the men must still suffer and have learned to bear pain. “I am inclined to think” marks a guess, not a test; readers might also weigh the smoke, which he says cannot cover the whole body.
evidence: I am inclined to think that slow and deliberate motion, and no attempt at escape, are perhaps the best safeguards
Still they must often suffer, but they are used to the pain

readings.title: Why Timor has no kangaroos — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow an argument from something that is missing, and test whether the absence proves what Wallace says.
readings.focus: Wallace argues from Timor’s few mammals that the island was never joined to Australia, and that its animals arrived by rare accidents across the sea.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Timor lies at the eastern end of a chain of islands running from Java towards Australia, about three hundred miles from the Australian coast. Wallace found that its birds came partly from Java and partly from Australia, and asked how any animals reached it. Mammals feed their young on milk; marsupials, such as kangaroos and opossums, carry their young in a pouch and are typical of Australia; the Latin names, such as Macacus cynomolgus, are the scientific names of species; corroborative means supporting; to dissever is to separate; a hacienda is a ranch; Oceanic Islands rose from the sea and were never part of a continent, and Charles Darwin argued that their animals arrived across the water; flotsam and jetsam are floating wreckage; gratuitous means unnecessary; Secondary, Eocene and Miocene are names for very ancient periods of the earth’s history.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XIV, “The Natural History of the Timor Group,” from the mammals of Timor to the end of the chapter; opens “The Mammalia of Timor as well as those of the other islands of the group are exceedingly…”; closes “…Since such last elevation, I feel confident that Timor has not formed part of Australia.”.

questions.prompt: Wallace lists Timor’s seven land mammals. What is missing from the list, and why does that matter to his argument?
facilitatorNotes: Not one is Australian. If Timor had once been part of Australia, “some kangaroo or other marsupial” would almost certainly be there. He argues from absence: what we would expect to find and do not.
evidence: not one of these species is Australian, or nearly allied to any Australian form
some kangaroo or other marsupial animal would almost certainly be found there

questions.prompt: How does Wallace explain the few mammals that did reach Timor?
facilitatorNotes: Over thousands of years, floods and eruptions carried trees out to sea, and once in a thousand or ten thousand years a lucky combination might carry an animal across. The deer may have been brought by people who keep tame fawns. Rare events become likely over very long times.
evidence: carrying out to sea hundreds of forest trees
once in a thousand, or ten thousand years

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace refuse to count the horses of Timor as wild animals?
facilitatorNotes: Every pony has an owner: they are domestic, like cattle on a ranch, whatever people believe. He counts only what the evidence supports, and leaves out a popular belief that has “no grounds whatever.”
evidence: there are no grounds whatever for such a belief
The Timor ponies have every one an owner

questions.prompt: Critics mocked Darwin’s idea as the “flotsam and jetsam theory.” Why does Wallace think Timor gives “the most positive evidence” for it? Is he convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Timor’s animals are a “miscellaneous” mix, as chance arrivals would be, and deep seas, sunken banks and volcanoes point to an island that rose on its own. He also limits his claim to recent times in the last paragraph. Students may find the argument strong or want more evidence; ask what evidence would change their minds.
evidence: Their productions are of that miscellaneous character which we should expect from such an origin
When I say that Timor has never formed part of Australia, I refer only to recent geological epochs.

readings.title: The Maleo’s eggs in the black sand — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow an argument from a bird’s body to its behaviour, and notice which steps are observed and which are reasoned.
readings.focus: Why a bird might leave its eggs to sun-warmed sand, and why Wallace thinks such habits can be explained at all.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. In the north of Celebes (now Sulawesi) he camps with a hunting party on a remote beach of black volcanic sand. The Maleo is a large ground bird found only there; its relatives the Megapodii and Talegalli (megapodes, or brush turkeys) bury their eggs in great heaps of earth and leaves. Incubation is keeping eggs warm until they hatch; a casque is a helmet-like bump. “Variation” and “natural selection” were the terms of the theory of evolution that Darwin and Wallace first published together in 1858.
readings.contentNote: Wallace shoots Maleos for specimens and mentions dissecting the females; his companions hunt wild pigs. The eggs are collected and eaten.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XVII, “Celebes,” from the camp on the Maleo beach through Wallace’s explanation of the bird’s habits; opens “Arrived at our destination we built a hut and prepared for a stay of some days, I to…”; closes “…structure, and by means of "variation" and "natural selection" both are kept in harmony.”.

questions.prompt: How does Wallace explain the black sand of this beach, and what detail supports his idea?
facilitatorNotes: He proposes an ancient lava stream from the Klabat volcano that has broken down into sand, and points out that the beaches beyond the small rivers on either side are white. The contrast in colour is his supporting clue.
evidence: We have here probably an ancient lava stream from the Klabat volcano
the beaches beyond the small rivers in both directions are of white sand

questions.prompt: How does Wallace know that a Maleo can carry only one large egg at a time?
facilitatorNotes: The eggs are so large that the body could hold only one, and in every female he shot the other eggs were no bigger than peas. The conclusion rests on dissection as well as on the size of the eggs.
evidence: it is not possible for the body of the bird to contain more than one fully-developed egg at the same time
none of the eggs besides the one large one exceeded the size of peas

questions.prompt: Wallace says the parents “neither do nor can watch” their eggs. What reasons does he give?
facilitatorNotes: Many hens lay in the same hole, so none could know its own egg; and hundreds of large birds living on fallen fruit could not all find food near one beach. Chicks that run off, and perhaps fly, on the day they hatch fit a life without parents.
evidence: would render it impossible for each to distinguish its own
many would perish of hunger

questions.prompt: What does Wallace criticize in the usual way of explaining instincts, and what does he propose instead?
facilitatorNotes: Writers treated habits as fixed and said bodies were designed to fit them, which ends inquiry. Wallace reverses the direction: the huge eggs and weak, sand-scratching feet help explain the habit, and habit and structure stay matched through variation and natural selection. Readers may find this convincing or note that he offers a probable account (“I think”), not a proof.
evidence: This assumption is however an arbitrary one, and has the bad effect of stifling inquiry
will often, as in this case, throw much light on the origin of its habits and instincts

readings.title: The strange beasts of Celebes — excerpt
readings.challenge: Weigh several explanations for one strange feature and decide which fits the evidence best.
readings.focus: Celebes has few mammals, but most are found nowhere else; Wallace tests three explanations of the babirusa’s upward-growing tusks.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Celebes (now Sulawesi) is a large island shaped like a starfish, lying in the middle of the archipelago between Borneo and New Guinea. Wallace found that many of its animals have no close relatives on the islands around it. Mammalia are mammals and terrestrial ones live on land; “peculiar” here means found only there; Tarsius spectrum is the tarsier, a tiny big-eyed primate; a civet is a cat-like animal; callosities are hard pads of skin; an antelope is a horned grazing animal; canines and incisors are teeth; rattans are spiny climbing palms; the wart-hog is an African wild pig; Cuscus is a marsupial, an animal that carries its young in a pouch; an affinity is a family likeness.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XVIII, “Natural History of Celebes,” the account of its land mammals, from “The Mammalia of Celebes” to the squirrels and opossums; opens “The Mammalia of Celebes are very few in number, consisting of fourteen terrestrial…”; closes “…surrounding countries, but seem vaguely to indicate a relation to the African continent.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the mammals of Celebes surprising?
facilitatorNotes: There are very few, but eleven of the fourteen land mammals are found nowhere else, and the most interesting seem related not to their neighbours but, vaguely, to Africa. An island in the middle of the archipelago turns out to be one of its most separate places.
evidence: no less than eleven are peculiar
seem vaguely to indicate a relation to the African continent

questions.prompt: Why have naturalists argued over what kind of animal the anoa is?
facilitatorNotes: It mixes features: wild cow in size and look, but smaller than any other wild cattle and in some ways like African antelopes. Classifying an animal means deciding which features matter most, and here they point different ways.
evidence: whether it should be classed as ox, buffalo, or antelope
It is smaller than any other wild cattle

questions.prompt: Wallace weighs explanations of the babirusa’s upward tusks. What are the first two, and why does he reject them?
facilitatorNotes: Old writers said they were hooks to hang the head on a branch; a likelier idea was that they guard the eyes from thorns. He rejects the eye-guard idea because the female, who feeds the same way, has no such tusks: one fact undoes a good-sounding explanation.
evidence: Some of the old writers supposed that they served as hooks
the female, who must seek her food in the same way, does not possess them

questions.prompt: What is Wallace’s own explanation, and how do the beaver and rabbit help his argument? Is he sure?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks the tusks were once useful and worn down, but now grow on unchecked, as a rabbit’s teeth do when nothing wears them. He says only that he is “inclined to believe” it. Today scientists think the tusks matter in fights and displays between males, which fits the fact that only males have them, and Wallace’s own last sentence, about tusks “broken off as if by fighting,” points that way.
evidence: I should be inclined to believe rather, that these tusks were once useful
just as the incisors of the Beaver or Rabbit will go on growing

readings.title: Banda: a smoking volcano and a nutmeg garden — excerpt
readings.challenge: Follow a writer from what he sees to what it makes him think, and find the evidence he reads in rocks and dead trees.
readings.focus: Why a volcano is stranger than familiarity lets us feel, and how a tiny, dangerous island became valuable.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. The Banda Islands, a small volcanic group far east of Java, were the world’s chief source of nutmeg, a trade the Dutch government controlled. A fathom (a measure of depth) is six feet; Aden is a dry port in Arabia. Sulphureous means smelling of sulphur; an efflorescence is a powdery crust; basalt and lava are volcanic rocks; Ceram is a large island to the north. Mace, the red net around the nutmeg, is sold as a separate spice.
readings.contentNote: The steamer serves gin, beer and wine. Wallace describes earthquakes and a flood from the sea that destroyed houses and forest.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XIX, “Banda,” from the voyage on the Dutch mail steamer through the description of the nutmeg tree; opens “THE Dutch mail steamer in which I travelled from Macassar to Banda and Amboyna was a…”; closes “…pigeons of Banda, which digest the mace but cast up the nut with its seed uninjured.”.

questions.prompt: How does Wallace show that life on the Dutch steamer revolved around food and drink?
facilitatorNotes: He lists the refreshments by the clock, from six in the morning to eight at night, with bitters and beer in between. The long, exact timetable sets up his closing joke about the “gastronomical excitements” that relieve a dull voyage.
evidence: At six A.M. a cup of tea or coffee is provided for those who like it
so there is no lack of little gastronomical excitements to while away the tedium of a sea voyage

questions.prompt: Why, according to Wallace, do people fail to feel how strange a volcano really is?
facilitatorNotes: Knowing about volcanoes from childhood makes them seem ordinary, while a northern European’s whole experience teaches that the earth is solid and holds water, never fire. He argues that if volcanoes were reported for the first time from a distant country, no one would believe it.
evidence: The knowledge from childhood, of the fact that volcanoes and earthquakes exist, has taken away somewhat of the strange and exceptional character that really belongs to them
it would not be believed on any human testimony

questions.prompt: What evidence on the islands does Wallace use to reconstruct their past?
