facilitatorNotes: The rocks: coral limestone up to three or four hundred feet with lava and basalt above, suggesting the islands are fragments of a larger land broken up by volcanic forces. The recent past: a stand of dead but upright trees records the sea flooding in after an earthquake two years earlier. Both are traces read as records.
evidence: The larger island has coral rock to a height of three or four hundred feet, while above is lava and basalt
This was a record of the last great earthquake only two years ago

questions.prompt: Why are such small, earthquake-shaken islands so valuable? Which reasons are about nature and which about people?
facilitatorNotes: Nature: light volcanic soil, shade and rain in every month suit the nutmeg so well that it needs no manure and little care, while forced cultivation elsewhere failed. People: the value goes to the Dutch government through its control of the trade. Readers can discuss how geography and power combine.
evidence: they have been and still are of considerable value to the Dutch Government, as the chief nutmeg-garden in the world
which requires no manure and scarcely any attention

readings.title: Wallace defends the nutmeg monopoly — excerpt
readings.challenge: Take an argument apart: find its claim, its reasons, its comparison and the assumption underneath.
readings.focus: Wallace argues that the Dutch were right to keep the nutmeg trade to themselves, and the argument rests on more than its stated reasons.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Banda is a cluster of small volcanic islands in the Moluccas (now in Indonesia), once the world’s only source of nutmeg and mace. In 1621 the Dutch East India Company took the islands by force; most of the Bandanese people were killed, enslaved or driven away, and planters using enslaved labour took over the nutmeg gardens. The Dutch government kept the trade as a monopoly, and destroyed spice trees on other islands so that they grew only where they could be guarded. A monopoly is control of a trade by a single owner; capitalists are owners of large amounts of money; fiscal means to do with taxes; excise and customs are taxes on goods; “political economy” was the name for economics; supposititious means imagined. Banca (Bangka) is an island with tin mines.
readings.contentNote: Wallace argues that a “higher” race governing a “lower” one needs different economic rules, and he calls most of Banda’s people “mongrels”: racist ideas of his time, read here so that they can be examined. He does not mention how the Dutch took the islands.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XIX, “Banda,” from the nutmeg monopoly to the end of the chapter; opens “The nutmeg trade has hitherto been a strict monopoly of the Dutch Government; but since…”; closes “…species. A beautiful small fruit-dove, Ptilonopus diadematus, is also peculiar to Banda.”.

questions.prompt: What does Wallace claim about the Dutch nutmeg monopoly, and what reasons does he give?
facilitatorNotes: That it is “perfectly justifiable,” even a duty: a small country cannot keep distant colonies at a loss; nutmeg is not a necessity of life; the profits lower taxes for the whole Dutch population; and without the government a few rich owners would take the monopoly instead. Ask students to list the reasons before judging them.
evidence: There are cases in which monopolies are perfectly justifiable, and I believe this to be one of them.
the produce of the state monopolies saves them from the weight of a heavy taxation

questions.prompt: Wallace imagines gold found on “some small and barren island.” How does his comparison work, and what important difference does it leave out?
facilitatorNotes: If a nation found gold on an empty island, working it for the public would be fairer than a gold rush. But Banda was not barren or empty: it had people, whose land and trade were taken. The analogy quietly removes the islanders from the question. Students may find other differences too.
evidence: let us suppose that no gold existed in Australia, but that it had been found in immense quantities by one of our ships in some small and barren island

questions.prompt: Wallace answers critics by saying Britain’s own monopolies, such as the salt tax in India, were worse, and he challenges objectors to name any harm. Are these good arguments?
facilitatorNotes: Showing that someone else did worse does not prove that this policy was right, and a challenge is not evidence: he offers only his claim that “no one was materially or permanently injured.” The history of 1621 is the kind of harm his challenge ignores. Some students may still find his point about British hypocrisy fair.
evidence: it is the height of absurdity for us to affect indignation at the conduct of the Dutch
I challenge objectors to point out any physical or moral evils

questions.prompt: Wallace writes of a “higher” race governing a “lower” one, and calls Banda’s people “mongrels.” What assumption do these words reveal? Is there any careful observation in the same paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes that races can be ranked and that ordinary rules of fairness need not apply to people he ranks lower; “mongrel” is a word for dogs, applied to people. Yet he also argues that mixed peoples are “only examples of intermixture,” not halfway stages between races, which was a careful point for his time. Readers can hold both: the observation and the prejudice in which it is wrapped.
evidence: The true "political economy" of a higher, when governing a lower race, has never yet been worked out.
whereas they are only examples of intermixture

readings.title: Amboyna: a coral harbour and a python in the roof — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how Wallace tells a frightening discovery in the order he understood it, and weigh a sweeping judgment against what he actually reports.
readings.focus: A harbour full of living coral, a hut full of new beetles, and a guest in the roof.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Amboyna (now Ambon) is an island in the Moluccas; its town was one of the oldest European settlements in the East and was held by the Dutch. Wallace stayed three weeks in a hut on a new cacao plantation in the interior. Actiniae are sea-anemones and medusae are jellyfish; rattans are climbing palms; cacao trees give chocolate beans, and plantains (cooking bananas) shade them. Curculionidae, Longicorns and Buprestidae are families of beetles; Papilio ulysses is a large blue swallowtail butterfly; Macassar is a port on Celebes and the Aru islands lie far to the east. Bouru (Buru) is a nearby island. Wallace’s “boys” are young men he employed to skin birds.
readings.contentNote: Wallace calls the Amboynese “dreadfully lazy,” a sweeping prejudiced judgment. A python is killed by being swung against a tree and struck with a hatchet.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XX, “Amboyna,” from the crossing of the harbour to the killing of the python; opens “Having made arrangements to stay for three weeks at a small hut, on a newly cleared…”; closes “…long and very thick, capable of doing much mischief and of swallowing a dog or a child.”.

questions.prompt: Wallace says that “no description can do justice” to the harbour, and then describes it. Which details does he choose? Why does he call the corals “animal forests”?
facilitatorNotes: Corals, sponges and anemones covering the bottom, a landscape of rocks, chasms, hills and valleys, bright fishes and floating jellyfish. Corals are animals, though they grow like plants, so the bottom is a forest made of animals. For once, he says, reality beat what he had read.
evidence: offering a variety of stations for the growth of these animal forests
For once, the reality exceeded the most glowing accounts I had ever read of the wonders of a coral sea.

questions.prompt: Why does Wallace say that “only the entomologist” can understand his delight among the felled trees?
facilitatorNotes: The fallen timber swarms with beetles of brilliant colours, nearly all new to him and rare or unknown in European collections. An insect collector sees treasure in what others would call a hot, dead clearing. He admits his passion is a specialist’s.
evidence: Only the entomologist can appreciate the delight with which I hunted about for hours in the hot sunshine

questions.prompt: How does Wallace build suspense in the story of the snake? Trace what he heard, what he saw, and what he finally understood.
facilitatorNotes: A rustling over the thatch at night, which he ignores; next day “a large mass of something,” which he takes for a tortoise-shell; then it “suddenly resolved itself” into a coiled python. Only at the end does he link it to the noise and realise he slept directly under it. Telling events in the order he understood them lets the reader share the shock.
evidence: thought it must be a tortoise-shell put up there out of the way
and I had slept soundly all night directly under him

questions.prompt: At the start Wallace calls the Amboynese “dreadfully lazy.” Does the rest of the passage support that judgment?
facilitatorNotes: He gives no evidence beyond his trouble in hiring a boat. The people he actually shows are mostly at work: half a dozen plantation labourers come at once, and one, a man from Bouru, catches the python “in a businesslike manner.” One complaint is thin evidence for a whole people’s character, a useful lesson in testing generalisations.
evidence: for the Amboynese are dreadfully lazy
proceeded to work in a businesslike manner

readings.title: Shells, boils and bread-fruit at Amboyna — excerpt
readings.challenge: Notice how Wallace explains causes, and how he describes something his readers have never tasted.
readings.focus: On a small island of the Spice Islands, Wallace admires a great shell collection, suffers weeks of boils, and finds the best vegetable he ever ate.
readings.context: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), an English naturalist, spent eight years (1854–1862) collecting animals and plants in the islands between Asia and Australia; The Malay Archipelago (1869) is his account of those travels. Amboyna (now Ambon) is a small island in the Moluccas, the Spice Islands, which the Dutch then ruled. Wallace stayed there several times between 1857 and 1860, once in a hired house to pack his collections for the ship to England. An ichthyologist studies fish; Mactras and Ostreas are clams and oysters, and cones, cowries and olives are kinds of shell; pith is light, spongy plant material; an isthmus is a narrow neck of land between two seas; praus are Malay boats; a spring-tide is an extra-high tide; a chafer is a beetle; acari are mites; Shadrach, Meshach (here “Mesach”) and Abednego are three young men in the Bible’s Book of Daniel; to propagate a plant is to grow new ones, and cuttings are pieces that grow roots; Ward’s cases were sealed glass cases for carrying living plants by ship; Covent Garden was London’s great fruit and vegetable market.
readings.contentNote: Wallace describes painful boils caused by mites. He uses “natives,” a word of his time.

excerpt.locator: Volume I, Chapter XX, “Amboyna,” from the collection of shells and fishes to the end of the chapter; opens “I went on Sunday, by invitation, to see a collection of shells and fish made by a…”; closes “…boat to Wahai on the north coast of Ceram, and thence to the unexplored island of Mysol.”.

questions.prompt: Wallace says common Amboyna shells are sold in London for a penny, though on Amboyna “they cannot be bought so cheaply.” How could that be?
facilitatorNotes: He gives clues rather than a full answer: shells have long been traded, so many are shipped in bulk; every visitor buys some, so local sellers can charge more; and common sorts have “lost all value” to collectors at home. Accept any explanation that uses these clues.
evidence: sold in the streets of London for a penny each
where they cannot be bought so cheaply

questions.prompt: Why is the canal at Paso not finished, and how do boats cross the isthmus instead?
facilitatorNotes: The thirty yards of sand are dragged across by hand, because every spring-tide would throw up a new sand-bank and block a canal. Wallace explains a strange arrangement by its cause.
evidence: all small boats and praus can be easily dragged
every spring-tide would throw up just such a sand-bank as now exists

questions.prompt: How do Wallace and Charles Allen describe the taste of bread-fruit? Why do they use so many comparisons?
facilitatorNotes: Yorkshire pudding, mashed potatoes and milk, something between dumplings and batter-pudding: English readers have never tasted bread-fruit, so the writers build it out of familiar foods. The two different comparisons also admit that taste is personal.
evidence: I compared it to Yorkshire pudding; Charles Allen said it was like mashed potatoes and milk
something in consistence between yeast-dumplings and batter-pudding

questions.prompt: Amboyna gave Wallace few specimens and weeks of painful boils. Why does he still call it “a bright spot” in his travels?
facilitatorNotes: It was where he first met the glorious birds and insects of the Moluccas, which make them “classic ground” for a naturalist. A place can matter for what it begins, not for what it yields.
evidence: not altogether very profitable to me in the way of collections
it was there that I first made the acquaintance of those glorious birds and insects
